whatTheComponentNOWexpresses.shape: a discriminated union on the props. Arm one is the previous component unchanged: source required, detail optional. Arm two adds secondClaim, a pair of source and detail where BOTH are required, and makes the top-level detail required.
whatTheComponentNOWexpresses.emitted: b source, sep, b secondClaim.source, sep, detail, sep, secondClaim.detail

whatItREFUSES: a second figure with no counting rule of its own. ProvClaim.detail is not optional.
a second figure while the FIRST figure has no counting rule. detail is required on the two-claim arm, so a call with source and secondClaim and no detail does not compile.
a third claim. There is no prop for one. The product ships none, so a case built on it could never fail for the right reason.
reordering the interleave. The order is emitted by the component and is not a prop.
whatItDOESNOTrefuse_statedRatherThanOmit: a single-figure chip with no detail at all. Eleven shipped instances are bold-only labels rather than figures, so requiring a rule on every bold slot would make the shipped form unrepresentable.
a group basis or a per-figure basis line. Prov carries no basis slot and the product puts none inside a prov chip.

any assertion about whether the two figures are consistent with each other. A React component cannot type-check the relationship between two values, and DEV_PROCESS rule 0 says a control that depends on someone remembering is not a control.

theTrapNAMEDratherThanBURIED.what: secondClaim.source renders next to source and secondClaim.detail renders at the far end, so the reading order of the props is not the reading order of the output.
theTrapNAMEDratherThanBURIED.why: that is the PRODUCT shape. A wrapper that tidied it would render markup the product does not serve, which src/status.tsx already names as the one thing this package must never do.
heldNotDocumented: test/law.test.mjs asserts the exact rendered order with four distinguishable sentinels and asserts the separator count
a markup-parity case compares against the shipped .nav-foot .prov, selected through the .nav-foot ancestor rather than by an index into the 33 prov elements on the page
two prove:gates injections, one on the interleave and one on the type

theProvContractLANDED.whyNOTaClaimsArray: an array of figure-and-rule pairs reads as figure, rule, figure, rule and would either render markup the product does not have or need a silent reordering step inside the component. It would also make N claims representable when the product ships at most two, and a case with no product counterpart cannot fail for the right reason.

theSecondContractChange.whyItIsNotAOneTokenFix: G-95 raised the level for WCAG 1.3.1 and 2.4.6 and dropped h5 from the stylesheet selector in the SAME commit, deliberately, so a re-introduced skip renders unstyled rather than looking correct. The kit was emitting an element the vendored stylesheet no longer paints, and gate 3 counts CLASSES so it could never have seen that. The only thing that caught it here was a markup-parity case that exists for one screen.
theSecondContractChange.howItIsHeldNow: test/law.test.mjs reads the heading element OUT OF vendor/shell.css, with comments stripped first because the G-95 comment block discusses h5 and h1 in prose, asserts exactly one heading element is styled under .state, and asserts the component renders that element. Nothing is pinned. A future re-vendor that moves the level turns the kit red.
theSecondContractChange.rule: DEV_PROCESS 2.4. One rule with two implementations needs a divergence test rather than two careful edits.

twoInjectionsThatWereWRONG.why: recorded rather than quietly fixed, because in both cases the first draft would have shipped a gate that could not fire and the PR body would have claimed it as coverage.

one.case: law: two claims two rules - the second provenance figure can arrive with no counting rule
one.firstDraft: aimed at test/law.test.mjs with the needle secondClaim?: never
one.result: SILENT. Relaxing a required prop to optional changes no rendered output and no source string that suite asserts, so the law suite passed on the injected tree.
one.correction: re-aimed at test/consumer.test.mjs, whose MUST_NOT_COMPILE harness compiles a forbidden program against the packed tarball. The needle is the offending case's own id, so a compiler failing for an unrelated reason cannot score as this gate working.
one.generalization: the only instrument that can see a TYPE get weaker is one that compiles against it. A law test that reads source strings and rendered output is blind to a relaxed optionality.

two.case: law: two claims two rules - a chip can carry a second counting rule while the first figure has none
two.firstDraft: collapsed the union to the one-claim arm
two.result: SILENT with a build error. A case that cannot build proves nothing.
two.correction: relax the two-claim arm's detail to optional instead, which compiles and lets the consumer case go green where it should be red.

twoInjectionsThatWereWRONG.harnessNote: scripts/prove-gates.mjs already throws when a mutation is a no-op, so a mutation that matched nothing could not have produced a false SILENT. Both of these were real behaviours of the injected tree, not harness artifacts.

adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.question: does the internal cast in Prov weaken the public type?
adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.answer: no, and it is not taken on trust. The cast is on the destructure only; the exported signature is ProvProps. The consumer test compiles two forbidden programs against the PACKED TARBALL and its generated .d.ts, and both injections that weaken the type were watched turning that gate red. If the cast had leaked into the public surface, neither injection could have fired.

adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.question: does exporting ProvClaim and ProvProps move the component count?
adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.answer: no. The counting rule is exports of dist/index.mjs where typeof is function; a type is erased at runtime. Measured after the change: 86. The gallery-completeness gate uses the same filter, so it is not dodged either.

adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.question: is the new markup-parity case able to fail?
adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.answer: yes, watched. An ad-hoc injection dropping the b wrapper from secondClaim.source turned BOTH the new case and the composed sidebar red, 23 tests 21 pass 2 fail, and was reverted. That revert also reverted uncommitted work in the same file, which was re-applied and re-verified green before anything was committed. Named because a silent partial revert is exactly the kind of thing that ships half a change.

adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.question: was the coverage assertion weakened, or was any class parked?
adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.answer: no. It never went red, so there was nothing to weaken. No exclusion set exists, no class is parked as structural, and the assertion is byte-identical to what it was on main.

adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.question: did gate 2 fire on this lane's own work?
adversarialReviewOfThisLanesOWNwork.answer: yes, and it was correct. A doc comment in src/status.tsx named a pixel gap and gate 2 flagged it at src/status.tsx:111 as a hardcoded value. The comment was reworded rather than the gate relaxed. Worth recording as a gate proving itself on live work rather than only under injection.
